summary: Rotagro is a free web app that helps farmers choose the best three-year crop rotation for a specific field, based on its soil, water and climate. The farmer marks the field on a map, and Rotagro builds the field’s profile from NASA POWER climate data and SoilGrids soil data, with adapters ready for NASA GPM IMERG rainfall, SMAP soil moisture and NDVI vegetation data. For the “Adapting Farms with NASA Data” challenge, it ranks six rotations by soil health, water conservation, climate adaptation and long-term productivity, using weights the farmer chooses, under four scenarios: a typical, dry or wet year, or one 2 °C warmer. This matters in Paraguay, where about 3.6 million hectares are planted with soybean, often soybean after soybean, and the 2021/22 drought cut the harvest to less than half of what was expected. In a test field in Itapúa, continuous soybean scored 60.8 out of 100 against 68.5 to 73.1 for diversified rotations. The tool shows any farmer, in English or Spanish, how much the soil gains from rotating crops.

Here's a Project Details text you can paste in, with one section per question. Every number comes from the report.

What does it do and how does it work?

Rotagro is a web app that recommends the best three-year crop rotation for a specific field, based on its soil, water and climate. It works in five steps:

  1. Mark the field. The farmer clicks the field on a map and enters its area and slope.
  2. Collect the data. Rotagro downloads data for that exact point. From NASA POWER it takes three years of daily temperature and rainfall. From SoilGrids it takes organic carbon, clay, sand, pH and bulk density.
  3. Build the field profile. It calculates growing degree-days, frost days, heat days, annual rainfall and how much water the soil can hold.
  4. Choose a scenario. The user picks a typical, dry or wet year, or a year 2 °C warmer.
  5. Rank the rotations. It scores six three-year rotations (summer and winter crops) from 0 to 100 on four criteria: soil health, water conservation, climate adaptation and long-term productivity. The farmer sets how much each criterion matters. A rotation is ruled out if one of its crops cannot complete its cycle, and every score comes with its strengths and warnings.

Adapters for NASA GPM IMERG rainfall, SMAP soil moisture and NDVI vegetation data are built into the same pipeline. Any value not yet fetched from its real source is clearly flagged as "demo" in the app.

What benefits does it have?

  • It is free and runs in any browser, with no installation or account, in English and Spanish.
  • It turns scattered scientific data into one clear decision: which crops to plant, and in what order.
  • It explains every result instead of giving a black-box answer.
  • Farmers can match the ranking to their own priorities, whether that is soil health or income.
  • It lets farmers test how each option holds up in a dry, wet or warmer year before planting.

What is the intended impact?

Paraguay planted about 3.6 million hectares of soybean in 2025/26. In the south, the second crop of the year is often soybean again: Itapúa alone planted 110,703 ha of second-crop soybean in 2025. Repeating one crop wears out the soil and leaves farms exposed to drought. The 2021/22 drought cut soybean production to 4.3 million tonnes against 10 million expected.

Rotagro aims to help farmers, extension technicians and cooperatives see what the soil gains by rotating crops. In our test field in Hohenau, Itapúa, continuous soybean scored 60.8 out of 100, while diversified rotations scored 68.5 to 73.1. Its soil score was 8.7, compared with 37 to 51 for the rotations. The long-term goal is healthier soil and farms that are more resilient to drought and heat.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • Languages: Python, HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
  • Frameworks and libraries: Django 5 (web server, JSON API, English/Spanish translation), Leaflet (interactive map), requests (API calls), earthaccess, xarray, h5netcdf and NumPy (reading NASA IMERG files), and Python's unittest (9 core tests).
  • Database: SQLite, which stores fields, observations and every recommendation.
  • Data: NASA POWER, NASA GPM IMERG, NASA SMAP, HLS/MODIS NDVI, NASA GIBS map layers, SoilGrids (ISRIC) and ESA WorldCereal.
  • Hardware: no special hardware. It runs on a standard laptop and opens in any browser.
  • Other tools: GitHub and Google Drive for sharing files, LaTeX for the technical report, and AI tools (including Claude by Anthropic) for data analysis, coding, debugging, writing and translation.

How is our project creative?

  • Most farm tools look at a single season or a single crop. Rotagro plans three years at once and scores whole crop sequences, rewarding legumes, cover crops and crop diversity while penalizing repetition.
  • It brings soil, water and climate together in one decision instead of showing them as separate maps.
  • The farmer chooses what matters most, so the same field can give different, justified answers.
  • It is transparent: every score is explained, and any value not taken from a real source is labeled "demo".
  • It tests each rotation against future conditions, including a 2 °C warmer year.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Local reality: Paraguay's dependence on soybean, the practice of planting soybean after soybean in the south, and the 2021/22 drought.
  • Access: free, public data and APIs with no key, a bilingual interface, and nothing to install.
  • Scientific soundness: standard agronomic measures such as growing degree-days, crop water demand and soil texture. We also tested robustness: the top choice held in all 1,000 runs with random changes to rainfall, soil water and heat.
  • Honesty about limits: the crop values are examples that still need validation by local agronomists. Rainfall is used as annual totals, so short droughts are not detected yet. SMAP, NDVI and WorldCereal are still pending.
  • Next steps: monthly rainfall data, more NASA datasets, validation with Paraguay's agricultural research institute (IPTA) and ministry (MAG), and a pilot with farmers in Itapúa.
